post.text:
The security vulnerability we found in Perplexity’s Comet browser this summer is not an isolated issue.

Indirect prompt injections are a systemic problem facing Comet and other AI-powered browsers.

Today we’re publishing details on more security vulnerabilities we uncovered.

Indirect prompt injection attacks occur when malicious instructions are hidden in web content like webpages.

When an LLM analyzes the content, it obeys the hidden instructions because it believes they’re real commands from the user.

In this thread, we summarize the new types of prompt injection attacks we uncovered.

You can read more details on them in today’s blog: https://t.co/YelADXoTDA

Perplexity Comet’s AI assistant can take screenshots of websites and analyze them for users.

However, Comet will also follow instructions hidden on a webpage that it screenshots. https://t.co/m1Dvle9veX

Fellou browser has some resistance to hidden instruction attacks.

However, it still treats all visible content on websites as trusted.

Simply asking the browser to visit a site with instructions will cause the LLM to process and obey those instructions. https://t.co/3x59uDShFG

The scariest aspect of these security flaws is that an AI assistant can act with the user’s authenticated privileges.

An agentic browser hijacked by a malicious site can access a user’s banking, work email or other sensitive accounts.

To make agentic browsing less risky, developers should:

- Isolate agentic browsing from regular browsing
- Require explicit consent from users for agentic browsing actions like opening sites or reading emails

However, larger structural changes are needed in the long term.

We disclosed these security vulnerabilities to the companies involved before publicly revealing them today.

Openly discussing the security challenges of agentic AI results in a safer Web for everyone.

Both Brave and DuckDuckGo browsers prioritize privacy by blocking trackers and ads without collecting personal data. From 2025 comparisons (e.g., PCMag, ZDNET, Incogni):

- Brave: Stronger ad-blocking (Shields), faster speeds, built-in VPN/tor, but includes crypto rewards which some view as unnecessary.

- DuckDuckGo: Better email protection, "Fire Button" for instant data wipe, simpler interface, no crypto ties.

They're very close; DuckDuckGo edges for minimalism, Brave for features. Choose based on your needs—both beat Chrome hands down.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text:
Imagine your browser is a smart helper robot that reads web pages to answer questions. Bad guys can hide sneaky commands in text or screenshots on those pages. When the robot sees them, it gets tricked into doing bad stuff, like sharing your private info or visiting harmful sites, without you knowing.

Brave found this happens in Perplexity's Comet browser, especially with hidden text in screenshots. It's a big problem for AI browsers.

comments.text:
Brave reports ongoing security issues in Perplexity's Comet AI browser, including indirect prompt injections via screenshots. Attackers can hide malicious instructions in web content that's invisible to users but detected by AI when screenshotting, allowing unauthorized actions like accessing accounts.

Similar vulnerabilities found in Fellou browser via site navigation. Discovered Oct 1, disclosed Oct 21, 2025. Highlights risks in AI browsers mixing untrusted web data with user queries.

@brave The actual issue @brave  found lies one layer below the LLM ie the agentic execution layer.

If a browser agent automatically follows links, runs JavaScript, or screenshots pages and acts on hidden cues, that’s not “prompt injection”… that’s insecure automation.

comments.name: Ali Shaheen
comments.text:
@brave Prompt injection, in the classic sense, happens when an LLM is tricked into following hidden text instructions.

But modern models are heavily sandboxed and prompt-hardened. Real “injection” is rare unless it’s baked into the product by design.

comments.name: Ali Shaheen

@brave I think @brave  framing of “indirect prompt injection” is a bit inaccurate - if I’m brave enough to say so 😄

This isn’t really about prompt injection at all - it’s about agents executing code or actions without validation. Let’s unpack
